title: Pair dal with rice or roti
body: Dal is high in lysine but low in methionine; rice and wheat are the opposite. Together they cover all nine essential amino acids.

title: You don't need to combine at one meal
body: Complementary proteins work across the whole day. Dal at lunch and curd at dinner still completes the profile.

title: Paneer is the density leader
body: About 18g protein per 100g — among the highest in Indian vegetarian food. A 100g block closes a big part of most protein gaps.

title: Soya chunks are a complete protein
body: Unlike most plant foods, soya needs no pairing — it has all nine essential amino acids on its own, at roughly 52g protein per 100g dry.

title: Moong dal digests easiest
body: Around 85% protein digestibility versus 65–70% for most other dals. Good choice on days your stomach feels heavy.

title: Total protein beats perfect timing
body: Research consistently finds daily total matters far more than hitting a specific window. Spread it across your meals and don't stress the clock.

title: Eggs are the reference standard
body: All nine essential amino acids in near-ideal ratio, and about as digestible as protein gets. Two eggs add roughly 12g.

title: Add curd to any meal
body: A cup adds around 7g protein and improves the amino acid profile of a dal-and-grain plate.

title: Seeds are the forgotten protein
body: Pumpkin, sunflower and sesame run 15–25g per 100g, plus zinc and magnesium. Easy to sprinkle on anything.

title: Protein protects muscle in a deficit
body: When calories are low, adequate protein is what keeps weight loss coming from fat rather than muscle.

title: Spread it, don't stack it
body: Roughly 20–40g per meal across the day supports muscle better than one large protein hit.

title: Chicken breast is the lean workhorse
body: About 31g protein per 100g cooked with very little fat — efficient when calories are tight.

title: Fish adds omega-3 with the protein
body: Rohu, surmai or salmon give you complete protein plus fats most Indian diets run short on.

title: Tofu for a dairy-free complete protein
body: Soy-based, so no pairing needed — useful when you're avoiding paneer and curd.

title: Sprouting improves absorption
body: Sprouting dal before cooking increases protein bioavailability and cuts antinutrients that block minerals.

title: Vary your dals through the week
body: Moong, masoor, chana, toor and urad have different amino acid and micronutrient profiles. Rotating them covers more ground than sticking to one.

title: You're well short today
body: Protein is under 40% of your target with the day mostly gone. A scoop of whey, 100g paneer, or two eggs closes most of it fast.

title: Quinoa and rajgira are complete
body: Both carry all nine essential amino acids without pairing — a swap worth knowing if you're bored of rice.

title: Most Indians run a protein shortfall
body: Typical intake sits around 40–45g a day against a need closer to 0.8–1g per kg bodyweight — and higher if you train.

title: Training raises the bar
body: Lifting regularly pushes protein needs toward 1.2–2.0g per kg bodyweight, well above the sedentary baseline.

title: You're over budget today
body: You've passed your calorie target. One day won't undo progress — get back to your normal pattern tomorrow rather than compensating hard.

title: You're eating too little
body: Well under target this late in the day. Chronic under-eating stalls fat loss by driving down energy and training quality.

title: A surplus is required to build
body: Muscle gain needs consistent extra calories. Under-eating on a bulk is the most common reason gains stall.

title: Liquid calories add up quietly
body: Juice, sweetened chai, and soft drinks contribute meaningfully without registering as a meal.

title: Ghee and oil are the hidden multiplier
body: A tablespoon is roughly 120 kcal. Two extra spoons across a day is often the whole difference between deficit and maintenance.

title: Weekly average beats daily perfection
body: Fat loss tracks your weekly total. One high day inside a good week changes very little.

title: Slow gaining stays leaner
body: A modest surplus builds nearly as much muscle as a large one, with far less fat along for the ride.

title: Eat enough to lift heavy
body: Strength work suffers first when calories run low. Fuel the session or the session won't progress.

title: Fiber is running low
body: You're under target. Dal, whole fruit, vegetables and whole grains are the easiest ways to close the gap.

title: Fiber keeps you full for free
body: High-fiber foods add bulk and slow digestion without adding many calories — useful when you're cutting.

title: Whole fruit over juice
body: Juicing strips the fiber that slows sugar absorption and keeps you satisfied.

title: Vegetables first
body: Starting a meal with the vegetable portion tends to reduce total intake without conscious restriction.

title: Increase fiber gradually
body: A sudden jump causes bloating. Raise it over a week and drink more water alongside.

title: You're behind on water
body: Well under target today. Thirst is a late signal — most people are already low by the time they feel it.

title: Hydration affects lifting
body: Even mild dehydration reduces strength output and makes sessions feel harder than they are.

title: Thirst can read as hunger
body: Having water before deciding you're hungry costs nothing and sometimes settles it.

title: Anchor water to habits
body: A glass with every meal and one on waking gets most people close to target without tracking each sip.

title: Heat and training raise your need
body: Indian summers plus a gym session can add a litre or more to what you actually need.

title: Log meals soon after eating
body: Logging within a few minutes keeps portions accurate. Recall at night is where most tracking error creeps in.

title: You've skipped a planned meal
body: You're behind your planned meal count for today. Skipping usually means a larger, less controlled meal later.

title: A late first meal compresses your day
body: Starting after noon leaves less room to spread protein and hit your calorie target comfortably.

title: Meal frequency is your choice
body: Two meals or six — when calories and protein match, results are similar. Pick what you can sustain.

title: Eat something before you train
body: A meal or snack in the few hours before lifting generally makes for a better session than training fully empty.

title: Nothing logged yet today
body: Log your first meal to unlock macro coaching. Even a rough entry beats no entry.

title: Consistency beats precision
body: A roughly-logged day every day tells you more than a perfectly-logged day once a week.

title: Log it even when it's off-plan
body: Skipping the entries you'd rather not see is what makes tracking stop working.

title: Slow down at the table
body: Fullness signals take time to register. Eating more slowly gives them a chance to arrive before you've overshot.

title: Serve, then sit
body: Plating your portion and putting the serving dish away removes the second helping decision entirely.

title: You're on track today
body: Calories, protein and hydration all where they should be. This is the pattern that produces results — nothing to change.

title: Weigh food while you learn
body: A few weeks on a scale calibrates your eye permanently. Most people over-estimate rice and under-estimate oil.

title: Plan tomorrow tonight
body: Deciding meals in advance removes the hungry-and-deciding moment, which is where most plans break.

title: Fermented foods support gut bacteria
body: Curd, buttermilk and idli batter feed gut bacteria and are staples you likely already keep at home.

title: Fermenting improves absorption
body: Idli and dosa batter ferment before cooking, which improves how well you absorb what's in them.

title: Variety feeds a better gut
body: A wider range of plants across the week supports more diverse gut bacteria than eating the same three vegetables.

title: Soak dal before cooking
body: Six to eight hours reduces phytic acid, which otherwise blocks mineral absorption from the same meal.

title: Pair iron with vitamin C
body: Lemon on dal or a citrus fruit alongside meaningfully improves iron absorption from plant sources.

title: B12 needs attention on a vegan diet
body: It's essentially absent from plant foods. Fortified products or a supplement is the standard route — worth discussing with a doctor.

title: Calcium beyond dairy
body: Ragi, sesame, and leafy greens carry meaningful calcium if you're not using milk or curd.

title: Don't fear the yolk
body: Yolks carry most of the egg's micronutrients. Whites-only discards the more nutritious half.

title: Fats aren't optional
body: Some dietary fat is needed to absorb vitamins A, D, E and K. Cutting it to near-zero works against you.

title: That meal leaned heavily on carbs
body: Adding a protein source to a carb-dominant plate improves both satiety and your macro balance.

title: Carbs fuel hard sessions
body: They're your main energy source for lifting. Cutting them too far usually shows up as weaker training.

title: Whole grains over refined
body: Bajra, jowar, and brown rice bring fiber and micronutrients that white rice and maida have lost.

title: Rice isn't the problem
body: Total calories drive fat loss, not any single food. Portion your rice rather than fearing it.

title: Sleep drives recovery
body: Short sleep reduces training quality and makes appetite harder to manage the next day.

title: Rest days build the muscle
body: Growth happens between sessions. Training through genuine fatigue slows progress rather than speeding it.

title: Eat on rest days too
body: Recovery has a fuel cost. Dropping intake sharply on non-training days undercuts the work you did.

title: Expect the scale to bounce
body: Daily weight swings on water and food volume. The weekly trend is the signal.

title: Steady loss holds better
body: Aggressive deficits cost more muscle and are harder to sustain than a moderate one.

title: Keep lifting while cutting
body: Resistance training during a deficit is what signals your body to keep muscle rather than burn it.

title: Progressive overload comes first
body: Nutrition supports growth, but adding weight or reps over time is what actually drives it.

title: Muscle gain is slow by nature
body: Real rates are measured in months. Rapid scale movement is usually mostly fat and water.

title: Strength needs recovery between sessions
body: Heavy work taxes the nervous system as much as the muscle. Spacing sessions is part of the programme.

title: Maintenance is an active skill
body: Holding a weight takes the same attention as changing it. The logging habit is what keeps it stable.
